introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Time allowed: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour, answer all questions): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State the first law of thermodynamics. *[2 marks]*

2.00 kg of water has a volume of $2.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$ when in the liquid state at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. When the water is completely changed from liquid to vapour at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, under a constant atmospheric pressure of $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, the volume increases to $3.38\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$.

(ii) How much work is done against the atmosphere as the water changes into vapour?

(iii) What is the change in the internal energy of the water during vaporization?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) First law of thermodynamics.** The increase in the internal energy of a system equals the sum of the heat supplied to the system and the work done on it: $\Delta U = Q + W_{\text{on}}$. Equivalently, $\Delta U = Q - W$, where $W$ is the work done **by** the system. (It is the law of conservation of energy applied to thermodynamic systems.)

**(ii) Work done against the atmosphere** (constant pressure):
$$W = p\,\Delta V = 1.01\times10^{5}\times(3.38 - 2.00\times10^{-3}) = 1.01\times10^{5}\times3.378$$
**$W = 3.41\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$.**

**(iii) Change in internal energy.** The heat supplied to vaporise the water at constant temperature is $Q = mL_v$. The data of the paper do not give $L_v$; the standard value for water at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $L_v = 2.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, is used:
$$Q = 2.00\times2.26\times10^{6} = 4.52\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$$
$$\Delta U = Q - W = 4.52\times10^{6} - 3.41\times10^{5} = 4.18\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$$

**$\Delta U \approx 4.2\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$ (4.2 MJ).** The temperature does not change, so this increase is in the **potential** energy of the molecules, which gain energy to separate against the intermolecular forces.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The graphs in *figure 5* show how tensile stress varies with tensile strain for two metallic wires, copper and steel. Study the two graphs and answer the questions that follow. The stress is applied until the material breaks, in each case.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

(i) Write down the breaking tensile stress of each of the materials.

(ii) Which of the materials is more ductile? Explain your answer.

(iii) Determine the Young modulus of each of the materials.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Breaking stress** (the stress at the end of each curve; readings $\pm0.1\ \mathrm{GPa}$):

- steel: about **$4.1\ \mathrm{GPa}$** (the curve ends at a strain of about 3 %);
- copper: about **$2.8\ \mathrm{GPa}$** (the curve ends at a strain of about 9 %).

**(ii) Copper is more ductile.** A ductile material undergoes a large **plastic** deformation (it can be drawn into wires) before it breaks. Both materials behave elastically (straight line) up to a strain of about 2 %, but copper then goes on stretching to about 9 % strain under an almost constant stress (a plastic extension of about 7 %), whereas steel breaks at about 3 % (a plastic extension of only about 1 %). Steel is stronger (higher breaking stress) but less ductile.

**(iii) Young modulus** = gradient of the initial straight line, $E = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}$.

- Steel: the line reaches a stress of $4.0\ \mathrm{GPa}$ at a strain of $2.1\ \%$:
$$E_{\text{steel}} = \frac{4.0\times10^{9}}{2.1\times10^{-2}} = 1.9\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa}$$
- Copper: the line reaches $2.6\ \mathrm{GPa}$ at a strain of $2.0\ \%$:
$$E_{\text{copper}} = \frac{2.6\times10^{9}}{2.0\times10^{-2}} = 1.3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa}$$

**$E_{\text{steel}} \approx 1.9\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, $E_{\text{copper}} \approx 1.3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa}$** (about $\pm10\ \%$, from the graph). The strain, a ratio, is converted from percent to a pure number before dividing.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State any two assumptions of the kinetic theory of matter used to derive the equation $P = \frac{1}{3}\rho\,\overline{c^{2}}$.

(ii) What is the name given to $\overline{c^{2}}$?

(i) What do you understand by the *electromotive force of a cell*?

In an experiment to determine the internal resistance of a battery, the current through a battery was made to vary with the voltage across a variable resistor as shown in *figure 7*.

![fig-2](gce-al-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_2.png)

Use the graph in figure 7 to determine:

(ii) the internal resistance of the battery;

(iii) the e.m.f. of the battery.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Electromotive force.** The e.m.f. of a cell is the **energy transferred (converted from chemical energy into electrical energy) per unit charge** that passes through the cell: $E = \dfrac{W}{Q}$, measured in volts. It equals the terminal p.d. when no current is drawn.

The terminal voltage obeys $V = E - Ir$, so a graph of $V$ against $I$ is a straight line of **gradient $-r$** and intercept $E$ on the $V$ axis.

**(ii) Internal resistance.** Take two well-separated points on the line of figure 7: $(35.0\ \mathrm{mA};\ 2.95\ \mathrm{V})$ and $(70.0\ \mathrm{mA};\ 2.24\ \mathrm{V})$.
$$\text{gradient} = \frac{2.24 - 2.95}{(70.0 - 35.0)\times10^{-3}} = \frac{-0.71}{0.0350} = -20.3\ \mathrm{V\,A^{-1}}$$
$$r = -\text{gradient} \approx 20\ \Omega$$

**(iii) E.m.f.** The graph does not reach $I = 0$, so use $V = E - Ir$ at a point on the line, e.g. $I = 35.0\ \mathrm{mA}$, $V = 2.95\ \mathrm{V}$:
$$E = V + Ir = 2.95 + (35.0\times10^{-3})(20.3) = 2.95 + 0.71 = 3.66\ \mathrm{V}$$

**$r \approx 20\ \Omega$ and $E \approx 3.7\ \mathrm{V}$** (readings from the graph, $\pm0.03\ \mathrm{V}$). The current axis is in mA: $35.0\ \mathrm{mA} = 35.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The three lowest energy levels of an atom are shown in *figure 8* below.

![fig-3](gce-al-physics-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_3.png)

(i) Determine the minimum energy in joules required to eject an electron initially in the lowest energy level from the atom.

(ii) Assuming that the energy level, $n$, is associated with energy $\dfrac{k}{n^{2}}$, determine the energy of the level $n = 4$ in electron-volts.

(iii) Determine the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation emitted when an electron makes a quantum jump from the level $n = 3$ to the level $n = 2$. Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum in which this radiation is found.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Constants: $1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$, $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

**(i) Ionisation energy.** To eject an electron from the lowest level ($n = 1$, $E_1 = -18.6\ \mathrm{eV}$) it must be raised to $0\ \mathrm{eV}$ (free electron):
$$E = 0 - (-18.6\ \mathrm{eV}) = 18.6\ \mathrm{eV} = 18.6\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 2.98\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}$$

**(ii) Level $n = 4$.** With $E_n = k/n^{2}$ and $E_1 = k = -18.6\ \mathrm{eV}$:
$$E_4 = \frac{-18.6}{4^{2}} = \frac{-18.6}{16} = -1.16\ \mathrm{eV}$$

**(iii) Transition $n = 3 \to n = 2$.** The photon energy is the difference between the two levels:
$$\Delta E = E_3 - E_2 = (-1.6) - (-6.2) = 4.6\ \mathrm{eV} = 4.6\times1.60\times10^{-19} = 7.36\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$$
$$\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{7.36\times10^{-19}} = 2.70\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$$

**$\lambda \approx 2.7\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ (270 nm).** This wavelength is shorter than $400\ \mathrm{nm}$: the radiation is in the **ultraviolet** region.

At resonance of the series circuit, the reactances are equal, $X_L = X_C$, and the impedance is a minimum, equal to the resistance $R$. Here $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi\times1.0\times10^{6} = 6.28\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

**(i) Capacitance.** $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, so
$$C = \frac{1}{\omega^{2}L} = \frac{1}{(6.28\times10^{6})^{2}\times200\times10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{7.90\times10^{9}} = 1.27\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{F}$$
**$C \approx 127\ \mathrm{pF}$.**

**(ii) Current.** At resonance $Z = R = 10\ \Omega$:
$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{0.10}{10} = 1.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{A}$$
**$I = 10\ \mathrm{mA}$ (r.m.s.).**

**(iii) Voltage across the inductor.**
$$X_L = \omega L = 6.28\times10^{6}\times200\times10^{-6} = 1.26\times10^{3}\ \Omega$$
$$V_L = IX_L = 1.0\times10^{-2}\times1.26\times10^{3} = 12.6\ \mathrm{V}$$
**$V_L \approx 12.6\ \mathrm{V}$ (r.m.s.).**

**(iv) Voltage across the capacitor.** $X_C = X_L$ at resonance, so $V_C = IX_C = 12.6\ \mathrm{V}$ (r.m.s.).

The voltages across $L$ and $C$ are equal in size but in antiphase, so they cancel in the series circuit, and both are about 126 times larger than the supply voltage of $0.10\ \mathrm{V}$ (voltage magnification). The resistance of the coil is neglected.
